doc.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Joining Chick Webb's orchestra and Webb's drumming
summary: Carter says Webb had an uncanny eye for musicians and a style of his own.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Well, I think the recordings belie such modesty. But, in any case, why don’t we move to another association after Fletcher Henderson, and that is Chick Webb.
Oh, yes. Dear, dear Chick Webb.
Do you recall the circumstances of joining that great orchestra?

No, but, gee, what . . . I don’t know how I happened to go . . . well, I guess he just offered me the chair in the orchestra. It’s interesting that Chick was not the musician that Fletcher Henderson was, but he had an uncanny feeling for good musicians, and everybody knew that, and you were really . . . oh, you were given a feeling of importance when he asked you to join his band, you know? And that’s with me, too. He had very good taste in music and in musicians, and he was some other kind of drummer, as you well know.
Could you contrast sort of the different musical styles of playing or the different demands on you playing in the two orchestras? Does anything come to mind that . . .

No, because I think if they called upon me to play something, they wanted me to play it the way I played it, you know, and I would attempt to also play it as the music is marked. As far as solos went, no one ever told me how to play a solo or even suggested, you know. I wish they had. [laughter]
Even I haven’t done that, and won’t. [laughter] Chick Webb is a drummer. You just alluded to his drumming.
What comments on his style can you make?
Gee, Chick was . . . I don’t know who I could say sounds like him today. He had a thing of his own, you know. I know that a lot of drummers tried to do what he did back then.
